title: The King Who Made Gold Lose Its Value

brand.cta: Follow The Black History Room for one story a day.

musa.commons: File:Catalan Atlas BNF Sheet 6 Mansa Musa.jpg

beats.text: In 1324, an African king brought so much gold to Egypt that gold itself lost value.

overlays.hook: He brought so much gold to Egypt, *gold itself lost value.*

beats.text: His name was Mansa Musa, king of Mali.
His empire stretched across West Africa, rich in gold and salt.

visual.title: Mali
visual.sub: one of the largest empires of its time

beats.text: In 1324, he crossed the Sahara on pilgrimage to Mecca.
Writers said tens of thousands travelled with him,
with camels each said to carry 300 pounds of gold.

visual.caption: Camels of a desert caravan, 19th-century print

beats.text: In Cairo, he gave gold to every official, and his people spent it freely.
So much gold flooded the city that its value fell.

visual.caption: Mansa Musa holding gold, Catalan Atlas, 1375

beats.text: A historian wrote that twelve years later, it still had not recovered.
A 1375 European map shows him on a throne, holding gold.
Back home, he brought architects and scholars, and built mosques in Timbuktu.
The city became a great center of Islamic learning.
Seven hundred years later, he is still called one of the richest people who ever lived.
His gold put Mali on Europe's maps. His scholars made Timbuktu a legend.

facts.claim: Mansa Musa's 1324 visit to Egypt (on hajj) brought so much gold that its value fell in Cairo.
Mansa Musa (Musa I), ruler of Mali in the 1300s.
facts.note: Reign dates differ: 1307 or 1312 to 1332 or 1337. Lower third says '1300s'.

facts.claim: Mali spread across West Africa; wealth from gold and salt; one of the largest empires of its time.
In 1324 he made the pilgrimage to Mecca, crossing the Sahara.
Contemporary Arab writers said tens of thousands travelled with him (60,000 in one report).
Camels reportedly each carried 300 pounds of gold.
facts.note: BRIT: 80 camels; NG: dozens. Script says 'each said to carry'.

facts.claim: He gave gold to court officials in Cairo and his people spent and exchanged gold.
The value of gold fell in Egypt.
About twelve years later it had still not recovered (al-Umari, writing c. 1336).
facts.note: Al-Umari is the only primary source for the 12-year figure; BRIT and NG repeat it. The script attributes it to 'a historian'.

facts.claim: The Catalan Atlas (1375) shows him enthroned holding gold.
He brought architects and scholars (including al-Sahili) and built mosques in Timbuktu.
Timbuktu became a major center of Islamic learning.
He is still often called one of the richest people in history.
facts.note: A reputation, not a measurement. The Catalan Atlas itself only calls him the richest king of his region.

notUsed: 'Richest person who ever lived' as a fact: his wealth cannot be measured; the script says he is 'still called one of the richest'.
'12,000 enslaved attendants' (BRIT): accurate per the chroniclers, but left out of a 60-second script to keep one fact per beat; mention in post text.
'He refused to kiss the ground before the sultan' (al-Umari only): not used.
